title: EEPA reports on Amnesty calls for investigation of attacks in Alamata
content:
BRUSSELS | 26 November 2026 (IDN | EEPA) — The following are the situation reports on the migration and refugee situation, the situation in Ethiopia, the situation in Sudan, the regional and international situation, Hundreds displaced in West Kordofan, Drone strikes in Blue Nile kill 19, Amnesty calls for investigation of attacks in Alamata.

  • At least 795 people fled Sudan’s Abu Zabad locality in West Kordofan state on 25 November, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). The displacement pushed residents mainly toward North Kordofan and East Darfur.
  • Denmark signed a letter of intent with Rwanda strengthening bilateral cooperation across multiple areas, including migration, signalling the next step toward establishing an offshore “return hub” in 2027. Denmark aims to finalize the agreement around the beginning of the new year.
  • The Democratic Republic of the Congo has urged five EU countries, including Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands, to reconsider plans for a Rwandan return hub, arguing that the agreement could indirectly support conflict and displacement in the Great Lakes region.

title: OPINION: Israel’s Arab Citizens May Save Israel from Itself
content:
Israel’s opposition leaders cannot chart a new course by preserving the politics of exclusion. Embracing Arab citizens as genuine partners is essential to democratic renewal and a future grounded in security and peace.

By Alon Ben-Meir*

NEW YORK | 25 November 2026 (IDN) — What should have been a watershed in Israel’s history is in danger of becoming another unforgivable betrayal. The result of the Israeli election offered an opportunity to end Netanyahu’s disastrous rule and begin rescuing the country from the political and moral abyss he has driven it into. Yet some opposition leaders appear more willing to perpetuate the exclusion of Arab citizens than to embrace the partnership that could make meaningful change possible—one that can open a new transformative chapter not only in the relationship between Israeli Jews and Israeli Arabs but also between Israel and the Palestinians.

title: A Christmas Carol for Capitalists? Dickens, Capra, and the Limits of Redemption
content:
By Sam Ben-Meir*

NEW YORK | 24 November 2026 (IDN) — Ebenezer, the newest film adaptation of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol, stars Johnny Depp in the eponymous role of Scrooge. The film has been called a “Christmas Carol for Capitalists” by David Crow, writing in Den of Geek—presumably because the poor are portrayed as dishonest, taking advantage of the well-off through fraudulent means, while those who seem to be acting on behalf of the poor are in reality lining their pockets with the charity of others. Or, like the unfortunate and generous-hearted Mr. Fezziwig, they wind up knifed to death by one of the underclass—a gratuitous act of violence, perhaps, and one not to be found in Dickens’ original story.

title: EEPA reports on RSF drone attack kills four in Khartoum
content:

  • A drone attack, suspected to have been launched by the Ethiopian National Defence Forces (ENDF), hit a vehicle in Adi Hara, Biyara kebele, Tahtay Adiyabo woreda, North-Western Tigray zone. At least four civilians were injured in the attack.
  • ENDF reportedly regained control of Biyara and Adi Asmerom, near Badme, over the weekend.
  • ENDF troops have been observed moving back and forth towards the Eritrean border near Badme while transporting military equipment, according to local sources. There are no reports of active fighting.
  • The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF)’s 35th, 11th, and 17th units joined the Eritrean Defense Forces in Gual Gemhalo, near Badme, according to local sources.
  • An ENDF drone attack on Badme forced an unspecified number of civilians to flee the town on 19 November.
  • Three drone strikes damaged the Abune Gebremeskel Monastery in Rama, Tigray on 20 November.

title: OPINION: Who Gets to Design the Future of Food Systems?
content:
The future of food systems should be shaped with the people whose lives depend on them.

By Neena Joshi*

KATHMANDU, Nepal | 23 November 2026 (IDN) — Tara Devi, a smallholder farmer from Muzaffarpur, Bihar, India, understands what it takes to make a farming household more resilient. As a Community Agro-Vet Entrepreneur (CAVE), she provides livestock health services and advice to 700–800 families in her community. Her work connects smallholder farmers with the knowledge and services they need to protect their livestock, improve productivity and strengthen their livelihoods.

But Tara’s experience also raises a bigger question about the future of food systems. Who gets to shape the solutions designed to transform them?

The development community has become increasingly sophisticated at designing solutions for a more resilient and sustainable food system. Blended finance, catalytic capital, climate finance, technology, regenerative agriculture and new investment models are giving us powerful tools to address complex challenges. Yet, for all our sophistication, we still too often design for communities rather than with them.

The future of food systems should be shaped with the people whose lives depend on them.

title: Arsenic in Thai Rivers Draws Scrutiny to Myanmar’s China-Linked Mining Trade
content:
By Jan Servaes

BRUSSELS | 22 November 2026 (IDN) — Arsenic detected in waterways in northern Thailand has prompted authorities to provide clean water to affected communities. Researchers traced some of the contamination to upstream gold mining in Myanmar. Reports of fish with sores in the Mekong have also raised concerns about food safety. Al Jazeera

On 16 November, the South China Morning Post reported on fish with visible sores in the Mekong. A few days earlier, environmental activist Aombun Thipsuna—chair of the Association of the Network of Community Organization Councils in the Seven Northeastern Mekong Basin Provinces—shared photos on social media of fish known locally as “pla khae,” which the local population has dubbed “zombie fish.” She told the Thai alternative news outlet Ejan that, since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, fishermen have increasingly encountered fish with such deformities.

According to Aombun, the “pla khae” can reach weights of up to 60 kg. As the fish is widely consumed in Thailand, this raises the risk of heavy metals entering the human food chain.

title: OPINION: Investigate the U.S. Envoy to Syria and Iraq
content:
By David L. Phillips*

OXFORD, UK | 20 November 2026 (IDN) — Tom Barrack’s handling of U.S. policy towards Syria deserves congressional scrutiny. So do reports that he advocated a role for a business associate’s firm in a major regional oil pipeline project. The House Foreign Affairs Committee should examine whether his diplomatic responsibilities and private business relationships were adequately separated.

An investigation should establish the facts without assuming its conclusion. Questions about impartiality deserve examination even where personal financial gain has not been demonstrated.

Reuters reported in October that Barrack promoted TI Capital, founded by his business partner Ziad Ghandour, for the Kirkuk–Baniyas pipeline project. Barrack disclosed a stake in ACD-TI Oakley Investment LLC, a separate property venture managed by TI Capital. Reuters found no evidence that he would profit from the pipeline. The State Department denied that he had a financial interest or role in the project and said he complied with ethics rules. (www.jpost.com

title: 2026 Water Conference: What’s at stake for Asia and the Pacific?
content:
By Lorenzo Santucci, Anshuman Varma, and Michael Koch*

BANGKOK, Thailand | 20 November 2026 (IDN) — As the global community gathers in Abu Dhabi for the 2026 United Nations Water Conference (December 8-10) to review progress and accelerate action towards SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation), the stakes for Asia and the Pacific are particularly high.

Despite important advances in recent decades, progress towards Goal 6 remains uneven and too slow to meet the 2030 targets. Climate change is adding further complexities through intensifying droughts, floods and water-related disasters across the region. In May, ministers, policymakers and stakeholders from across the region highlighted both the scale of the challenges and the opportunities to accelerate action. A clear message emerged: while the region remains off track on several SDG 6 targets, the region is home to innovative solutions and strong leadership that can help drive progress.

title: EEPA reports on EU deportations of rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda to start in 2027
content:

  • Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced on 16 November that the first group of around 100 rejected asylum seekers will be transferred to a pilot open facility in Rwanda by 2027. The details of the agreement are still being negotiated.
  • Ugandan Foreign Ministry Permanent Secretary Vincent Waiswa Bagiire affirmed that Uganda is also in talks with European countries, especially with the Netherlands, to potentially host a “return hub” for rejected asylum seekers.
  • 483 undocumented Eritrean migrants are detained at a smuggling site in Tripoli, Libya, linked to the kidnapping of five Eritreans, one of whom died as a result of torture. The South Tripoli Primary Prosecution Office has launched an investigation into the crimes.
  • A boat carrying migrants capsized 40km off the coast of Senegal, near Dakar. The boat carried up to 100 people, at least one of whom died in the accident.

title: ESSAY: Beyond the Hive — Freedom, Community, and the Rivals of Amziah King
content:
By Sam Ben-Meir*

NEW YORK | 18 November 2026 (IDN) — Andrew Patterson’s The Rivals of Amziah King (2026) appears at first to be a story about competition, community, and revenge. But beneath its exuberant musical performances, eccentric characters, and increasingly violent confrontations lies a more radical philosophical proposition: that human beings are capable of organizing their lives according to principles fundamentally different from those governing capitalist exchange. The film’s recurring images of honeybee colonies are crucial to this vision, as are its extraordinary scenes of communal music-making. Together, they suggest a conception of freedom that is neither individualistic nor hierarchical, but realized through relationships of mutual dependence, responsiveness, and care.
